subject: maths
title: Substitution Sanctuary
description: Use u-substitution to unlock tricky integrals.

concepts.def: Let u = inner function; rewrite integral in terms of u and du.
Often pick u as the 'inside' whose derivative appears.
For definite integrals, transform limits to u values too.
∫(2x+1)⁵ dx with u=2x+1, du=2dx; gives (2x+1)⁶/12 + C.
f'(x)·f(x)ⁿ, f'(x)/f(x), and e^(f(x))·f'(x) all substitution-friendly.

walkthroughs.body_html:
u = x²+1, du = 2x dx

∫ u³ du = u⁴/4 = (x²+1)⁴/4 + C

u = 3x, du = 3dx

(1/3)∫ cos u du = (1/3) sin 3x + C

u = x²+1, du = 2x dx

(1/2)∫ du/u = (1/2)ln|x²+1| + C

options: u = x²
u = cos x
u = x
u = 2x

mcqs.q: Can a definite integral give a negative value, even when integrating a function from left to right?
options: Yes — if the function is below the x-axis over the interval, the integral is negative.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.
Definite integrals are always positive because area cannot be negative.
The derivative of 5 is 1 because all constants differentiate to 1.

mcqs.q: What must you remember to include when finding an indefinite integral?
options: You don't need anything extra — the integral is just the antiderivative.
A constant of integration (+ C), because the derivative of any constant is zero.
You always need to add 1 to the answer to account for rounding.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.

mcqs.q: What is the derivative of a constant, like d/dx(5)?
options: The derivative of 5 is 1 because all constants differentiate to 1.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.
The derivative of 5 is 5 because the constant stays the same.
0 — constants do not change with x.

sequence.def: Substitution reverses the chain rule — the concept.
Pick an inner function u to substitute.
Find du/dx and replace dx with du.
Convert x-limits to u-limits for a definite integral.
Work a simple linear substitution example.
Recognise recurring forms for speed — final mastery.
